extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys and agents), OED staff, USPTO adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing investigations, sanctions, interim suspension, reciprocal discipline, settlement, exclusion on consent, disability inactivation, and procedural requirements for practitioners practicing before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for offensive papers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a paper is found to be offensive or improper, the USPTO Director may impose sanctions or actions, which may include any combination of striking the offending paper; referring a practitioner's conduct to the Director of the Office of Enrollment and Discipline; precluding a party or practitioner from submitting a paper, or presenting or contesting an issue; affecting the weight given to the offending paper; or terminating the proceedings in the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions are discretionary and may be combined. Practitioners who violate the provisions may also be subject to disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature requirement for correspondence (§11.18(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: For all documents filed in the Office in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters (except correspondence required to be signed by the applicant or party), each piece of correspondence filed by a practitioner must bear a signature, personally signed or inserted by such practitioner, in compliance with § 1.4(d) or § 2.193(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to documents filed with a hearing officer in a disciplinary proceeding as well; noncompliance can jeopardize the filing's probative value and may trigger sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification when presenting papers (§11.18(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: By presenting any paper (signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating), the presenting party certifies that (1) statements of the party's own knowledge are true, statements on information and belief are believed to be true, and (2) to the best of the party's knowledge, information, and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, the paper is not being presented for any improper purpose (e.g., to harass or cause unnecessary delay or needless increase in the cost of any proceeding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False statements may trigger criminal penalties under 18 U.S.C. 1001 and jeopardize the paper's probative value. The certification imposes an objective 'reasonable inquiry' standard on the filer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary jurisdiction scope (§11.19(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: All practitioners engaged in practice before the Office, practitioners administratively suspended, registered or recognized to practice in patent matters, resigned or inactivated under § 11.11, practitioners authorized under § 41.5(a) or 42.10(c), and practitioners transferred to disability inactive status or publicly disciplined by a duly constituted authority are subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Office. A non-practitioner engaging in practice before the Office without authority is also subject to disciplinary authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes who may be investigated and disciplined by the Office; jurisdiction includes a wide class of present and former practitioners and some non-practitioners acting without authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for discipline (§11.19(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds for discipline include, whether done individually or with others and whether or not in course of providing legal services or in a pending Office matter: (i) conviction of a serious crime; (ii) discipline on ethical or professional misconduct grounds imposed in another jurisdiction or disciplinary disqualification from participating in or appearing before any Federal program or agency; (iii) failure to comply with any court order disciplining a practitioner, or any final decision of the USPTO Director in a disciplinary matter; (iv) violation of any USPTO Rule of Professional Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds may be applied regardless of whether the conduct occurred in the Office matter; discipline elsewhere can form the basis for USPTO discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for transfer to disability inactive status (§11.19(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds for transfer to disability inactive status include: (i) being transferred to disability inactive status in another jurisdiction; (ii) being judicially declared incompetent, involuntarily committed after a hearing on grounds of insanity, incompetency or disability, or placed under guardianship or conservatorship by court order; (iii) filing a motion requesting a disciplinary proceeding be held in abeyance because the practitioner is suffering from a disability or addiction that makes it impossible to adequately defend the charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are distinct from misconduct grounds and relate to practitioner capacity/incapacity to practice or defend proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Director referral for unauthorized practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director may refer circumstances suggesting unauthorized practice of law to the appropriate authorities in the relevant jurisdiction(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a mechanism to address practice by unlicensed persons or practice beyond authorized scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of discipline available (§11.20(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: After notice and opportunity for a hearing, where grounds exist, the USPTO Director may impose: (1) exclusion from practice before the Office; (2) suspension from practice before the Office for an appropriate period of time; (3) reprimand or censure; or (4) probation (which may be in lieu of or in addition to other sanctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probation conditions must be stated in the order; violation of probation can lead to further discipline after notice to show cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions imposed with discipline (§11.20(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing discipline, the USPTO Director may condition reinstatement upon making restitution, successfully completing a professional responsibility course or examination, or any other condition deemed appropriate under the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions are flexible and tailored to circumstances; compliance (or lack thereof) affects reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer to disability inactive status procedure (§11.20(c) and §11.28)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director may transfer a practitioner to disability inactive status after notice and opportunity for a hearing where grounds exist to believe the practitioner has been transferred in another jurisdiction, judicially declared incompetent, involuntarily committed, or placed under guardianship or conservatorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfer may follow a hearing; subsequent rules (§11.28) govern motions to hold proceedings in abeyance and the specific documentary and medical evidence required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warnings (§11.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: A warning is neither public nor a disciplinary sanction. The OED Director may conclude an investigation with issuance of a warning, which shall contain a statement of facts and identify the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct relevant to the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings are administrative dispositions short of formal discipline; they identify the misconduct and applicable rules but are not public sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation initiation sources and scope (§11.22(a)-(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director is authorized to investigate possible grounds for discipline upon receiving a grievance, information, or evidence from any source suggesting possible grounds. Neither unwillingness nor neglect by a grievant to prosecute, nor settlement or restitution with the grievant, shall in itself justify abatement of an investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations can be initiated from any credible source; the OED Director retains discretion to proceed regardless of the grievant's actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for information and evidence during investigation (§11.22(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: During an investigation, the OED Director may request information and evidence from the grievant, the practitioner, or any person reasonably expected to provide needed information. The OED Director may request information from a non-grieving client only after practitioner consent or a Contact Member of the Committee on Discipline finds good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for and disclosure of non-grieving client information do not constitute a violation of USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct. Contact Members who assist in obtaining such information must recuse from probable cause panels concerning that practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary screening, notice, and disposition options (§11.22(d),(e),(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall examine all information or evidence concerning possible grounds; shall notify the practitioner in writing of initiation of an investigation; and upon conclusion may close the investigation, issue a warning, institute formal charges with Committee approval, enter a settlement agreement (subject to USPTO Director approval), or enter into a diversion agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigation disposition is discretionary but governed by standards; closing is required where information is unfounded, outside jurisdiction, not legally grounds for discipline, or insufficient to show probable cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee on Discipline composition and powers (§11.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director appoints a Committee on Discipline of at least three Office employees, none of whom shall report to the OED Director; each must be a member in good standing of the highest court of a State. Panels of three determine by majority vote whether there is probable cause to bring charges and prepare probable cause findings for the OED Director. Committee deliberations are confidential and members are not required to testify about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee independence from OED is required; panels act by majority vote and their deliberations are protected to promote candid review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline notice and prima facie effect (§11.24(a),(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 30 days of being publicly censured, reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended, or disciplinarily disqualified elsewhere, a practitioner must notify the OED Director in writing. Upon receipt or other learning of such discipline, the OED Director shall obtain a certified copy of the record or order, which establishes a prima facie case by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner was disciplined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A certified copy from another jurisdiction creates presumptive proof for USPTO proceedings; the OED Director may file a complaint predicated on that discipline without Committee authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Director procedure and defenses in reciprocal discipline (§11.24(b)-(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall issue a notice and order containing the record copy, complaint copy, and an order directing the practitioner to file a response within 40 days establishing a genuine issue of material fact that (i) the procedure elsewhere lacked notice or opportunity to be heard (deprivation of due process); (ii) there was such infirmity of proof as to make the Office unable to accept the conclusion; (iii) imposition of the same discipline would result in grave injustice; or (iv) arguments that the practitioner was not disciplined. If no genuine issue exists, the USPTO Director will impose identical discipline; if a genuine issue exists, the matter may be referred for a formal hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office generally gives effect to discipline elsewhere unless clear, specific defenses showing fundamental procedural or substantive inadequacy are established by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim suspension based on conviction of a serious crime (§11.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon conviction of a crime, a practitioner must notify the OED Director within 30 days. The OED Director determines if the crime is a 'serious crime'; if so, the OED Director may file proof and request the USPTO Director to issue a notice and order. The USPTO Director may place a practitioner on interim suspension after hearing the request on the documentary record. The practitioner is served with the certified court record, complaint, and ordered to respond within 40 days to establish genuine issues of material fact (e.g., crime not serious, practitioner not the individual convicted, deprivation of due process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings are handled expeditiously; the USPTO Director may terminate interim suspension for extraordinary circumstances and refers matters to a hearing officer for formal discipline after entering a final order imposing interim suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of conviction standard for interim suspension (§11.25(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A certified copy of the court record, docket entry, or judgment of conviction in a U.S. court (or foreign court, with some additional considerations) establishes a prima facie case by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner was convicted of a serious crime and that the conviction was not lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign convictions allow the practitioner to contest whether elements of a 'serious crime' are met under foreign law by clear and convincing evidence at the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement following conviction-related discipline (§11.25(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a practitioner suspended solely under interim suspension provisions demonstrates the underlying finding of guilt or conviction has been reversed or vacated, the interim suspension shall be vacated and the practitioner placed on active status unless the reversal/vacatur is partial. A practitioner convicted of a serious crime may petition for reinstatement no earlier than after completion of sentence, probation, or parole, whichever is later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vacating the interim suspension does not terminate other disciplinary proceedings unrelated to the vacated conviction; reinstatement timing is tied to completion of criminal sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement confidentiality and effect (§11.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before or after a complaint is filed, settlement conferences may occur; offers of compromise and statements made during settlement discussions are not admissible in subsequent proceedings. The OED Director may recommend settlement terms, including corrective or mitigating steps. A settlement agreement is effective only upon entry of a final decision by the USPTO Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement communications are protected from admissibility but require USPTO Director approval to become effective; corrective measures may be included as conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion on consent — affidavit and consequences (§11.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who desires to resign while subject to investigation or a pending disciplinary proceeding may only do so by consenting to exclusion and delivering an affidavit stating: consent is freely and voluntarily rendered; practitioner is aware of the pending investigation/charges (specified); and acknowledging that, if applying for reinstatement, the OED Director will conclusively presume that (i) the facts forming the basis of the investigation or complaint are true and (ii) the practitioner could not have successfully defended against the allegations. Upon approval, the USPTO Director enters an order excluding the practitioner on consent; excluded practitioners may not petition for reinstatement for five years and must comply with §11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion on consent carries presumptions adverse to later reinstatement applications and strict compliance obligations; failure to comply with §11.58 can be grounds to deny reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to hold disciplinary proceeding in abeyance for incapacity (§11.28(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may move to hold a disciplinary proceeding in abeyance alleging disability or addiction that makes it impossible to adequately defend charges. The motion must include: a brief statement of all material facts; affidavits, medical reports, official records, or other documents and the opinion of at least one medical expert establishing material facts; a statement acknowledging the alleged incapacity; written consent to be transferred to disability inactive status if granted; and written agreement not to practice before the Office while in disability inactive status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The motion must meet evidentiary thresholds; the OED Director has 30 days to respond (subject to enlargement) and must set forth objections and documentary evidence to dispute material facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of incapacity motion and conditions while in disability inactive status (§11.28(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The hearing officer shall rule on the motion; it shall be granted upon showing good cause to believe the practitioner is incapacitated as alleged. If granted, the hearing officer enters an order holding the proceeding in abeyance, the OED Director transfers the practitioner to disability inactive status, gives notice and publishes notice, and the practitioner must comply with §11.58 and may not engage in practice before the Office until a determination is made to resume practice. Permission for paralegal activity while inactive may be granted only if conditions of §11.58 are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orders for addiction may include conditions for return to active status; transfer triggers publication and Office notifications and imposes practice restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion for reactivation after disability inactive status (§11.28(b)-(c) and §11.29(b)-(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner transferred to disability inactive status in a disciplinary proceeding may file a motion for reactivation once a year beginning not less than one year after the initial effective date of inactivation (or more frequently if the order so provides). The motion alleging recovery must be accompanied by available medical reports or similar documents; the hearing officer may require additional information and may schedule the disciplinary proceeding to resume if reactivation is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reactivation requires objective medical documentation and is subject to hearing officer discretion; frequency of motions is limited by the inactivation order.
